questions.question_text: A distribution of incomes is strongly right-skewed. The best measure of center is the:
questions.option_a: mean, since it uses every value
questions.option_b: median, since it resists extreme values
questions.explanation: Right skew drags the mean above the typical value; the median resists outliers. 'Uses every value' is exactly why the mean fails here. Range isn't a measure of center at all.

questions.question_text: Adding 10 to every value in a data set changes the:
questions.explanation: Adding a constant shifts location (mean/median) but leaves spread unchanged — every point moves together, so distances are identical. Multiplying is what scales the SD.

questions.question_text: SAT scores are N(1050, 200). About what proportion score above 1250?
questions.explanation: 1250 is one SD above the mean. The empirical rule puts 68% within ±1 SD, leaving 32% in the two tails — 16% in the upper tail. Forgetting to halve gives 0.32.

questions.question_text: A z-score of −1.5 tells you the value is:
questions.explanation: A z-score measures distance from the mean in STANDARD DEVIATIONS, not raw units. This standardization lets you compare values from different distributions.

questions.question_text: A study finds r = 0.92 between ice cream sales and drownings. The best interpretation is:
questions.option_b: a strong positive association, likely from a lurking variable like temperature
questions.option_c: the correlation is too high to be real
questions.option_d: 92% of drownings are explained by ice cream
questions.explanation: Correlation ≠ causation; hot weather drives both. Option D confuses r with r²; even r² is 'variation explained,' never 'caused.' This lurking-variable setup is a perennial exam item.

questions.question_text: A regression line is ŷ = 12 + 3.5x. The residual for the point (2, 21) is:
questions.explanation: Predicted ŷ = 12 + 3.5(2) = 19; residual = actual − predicted = 21 − 19 = 2. A positive residual means the point sits above the line; reversing the subtraction gives −2.

questions.question_text: If r = 0.8, the coefficient of determination r² tells us:
questions.option_a: 80% of the variation in y is explained by x
questions.option_b: 64% of the variation in y is explained by the linear model
questions.option_d: 64% of points lie on the line
questions.explanation: r² = 0.64 = the fraction of variation in the response explained by the regression. It is NOT the slope or the percent of points on the line — those are different quantities entirely.

questions.question_text: A radio host asks listeners to call in about a tax proposal. This suffers most from:
questions.explanation: Call-in polls attract people with strong opinions — the sample selects itself. Nonresponse bias is different: it occurs when people CHOSEN for a sample fail to respond.

questions.question_text: Why does random ASSIGNMENT in an experiment permit cause-and-effect conclusions?
questions.option_a: it makes the sample represent the population
questions.option_b: it balances lurking variables across treatment groups on average
questions.explanation: Random assignment spreads confounders evenly between groups, so treatment is the only systematic difference. Representing the population is random SELECTION's job (generalization) — keep the two 'randoms' distinct.

questions.question_text: Dividing a school into grade levels and randomly sampling within each grade is:
questions.explanation: Strata = groups SIMILAR within, sampled from each (grades). Clusters = groups sampled WHOLE. The distinction: stratified samples from every group; cluster picks some groups entirely.

questions.question_text: Events A and B have P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A and B) = 0.2. They are:
questions.option_a: independent, since P(A and B) = P(A)·P(B)
questions.explanation: P(A)·P(B) = 0.5×0.4 = 0.2 = P(A and B) → independent. Mutually exclusive (nonzero) events are never independent — confusing the two is the standard trap.

questions.question_text: X has SD 2; Y has SD 1.5. If X and Y are independent, the SD of X − Y is:
questions.explanation: Variances ADD even when subtracting: Var(X−Y) = 4 + 2.25 = 6.25, SD = 2.5. Subtracting SDs (0.5) is the classic error; D is the variance, not the SD.

questions.question_text: Which scenario is a binomial setting?
questions.option_a: drawing 5 cards without replacement, counting hearts
questions.option_b: flipping a fair coin 20 times, counting heads
questions.explanation: Binomial = fixed n, independent trials, constant p, counting successes (BINS). Without-replacement breaks independence; 'until first success' is geometric; height is continuous.

questions.question_text: A player makes 80% of free throws. The probability the first MISS is on attempt 3 is:
questions.explanation: Make, make, miss = (0.8)(0.8)(0.2) — geometric, exact sequence, no coefficient. Option D adds a binomial coefficient, which belongs to 'exactly one miss in 3,' a different question.

questions.question_text: A population is strongly skewed (mean 50, SD 12). For samples of n = 36, x̄ is approximately:
questions.explanation: CLT: n = 36 ≥ 30 → x̄ is approximately normal regardless of population shape, with SD = σ/√n = 12/6 = 2. Forgetting to divide by √n (option B) is the most common error.

questions.question_text: Which condition lets you treat the sampling distribution of p̂ as approximately normal?
questions.explanation: For proportions, the large-counts condition (at least 10 expected successes AND 10 failures) governs normality — not the n ≥ 30 rule, which is for means. Each statistic has its own normality condition.

questions.question_text: A 95% confidence interval for a proportion is (0.42, 0.58). The correct interpretation is:
questions.option_a: 95% of the data lie in this range
questions.option_b: we are 95% confident the interval captures the true proportion
questions.option_c: there's a 95% chance the true p is in this interval
questions.explanation: Confidence is in the METHOD: 95% of intervals built this way capture p. Option C treats p as random, but p is fixed — the interval is what varies. This wording earns the point on FRQs.

questions.question_text: To halve the margin of error in a proportion interval (same confidence), the sample size must be:
questions.explanation: Margin of error scales with 1/√n, so cutting it in half requires 4× the sample size. The square-root relationship means precision gets expensive fast.

questions.question_text: Use a t-distribution instead of z for a mean when:
questions.option_b: the population standard deviation is unknown
questions.explanation: t replaces z whenever σ is estimated by s — nearly always in practice. The heavier t-tails account for the extra uncertainty of estimating σ. Sample size sets the degrees of freedom, not the z-vs-t choice.

questions.question_text: A test of H₀: μ = 100 vs Hₐ: μ > 100 yields P-value 0.03. At α = 0.05:
questions.option_c: the probability H₀ is true is 0.03
questions.explanation: P = 0.03 < α = 0.05 → reject H₀. We never 'accept' H₀ (only fail to reject), and the P-value is P(data this extreme | H₀ true), not the probability H₀ is true.

questions.question_text: Cholesterol is measured before and after a diet on the same 40 subjects. The correct test is:
questions.explanation: Before/after on the SAME subjects = paired data; analyze the 40 differences as one sample. A two-sample t-test wrongly assumes independent groups and discards the pairing.

questions.question_text: Which change increases the POWER of a test?
questions.explanation: Larger n shrinks variability, making real effects easier to detect. Lowering α makes rejecting harder (less power); two-sided tests split α across tails. Power rises with n, α, and effect size.

questions.question_text: A medical test uses H₀: patient is healthy. A Type II error means:
questions.option_a: telling a healthy patient they're sick
questions.option_b: telling a sick patient they're healthy
questions.explanation: Type II = failing to reject a false H₀ = missing the disease. Type I (option A) is the false alarm. Mnemonic: Type I cries wolf, Type II misses the wolf.

questions.question_text: A chi-square test of independence on a 3×4 table has how many degrees of freedom?
questions.explanation: df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1) = 2 × 3 = 6. Option A is the cell count; option B (cells − 1) is the df for a goodness-of-fit test with 12 categories — a different chi-square test.

questions.question_text: Which chi-square test compares the distribution of one categorical variable to a claimed model?
questions.explanation: Goodness-of-fit compares one sample's category counts to expected proportions (e.g., 'is this die fair?'). Independence and homogeneity use two-way tables; the t-test is for means, not categories.

questions.question_text: Regression output shows slope b = 2.8, SE = 0.9, n = 25. The t-statistic for H₀: β = 0 is about:
questions.explanation: t = (b − 0)/SE = 2.8/0.9 ≈ 3.11, df = n − 2 = 23. Option C inverts the ratio; D is a critical value, not a test statistic. Reading regression output is guaranteed exam content.

questions.question_text: A confidence interval for a regression slope that contains 0 suggests:
questions.option_b: no statistically significant linear relationship between x and y
questions.explanation: If 0 is a plausible slope, you can't rule out 'no linear association' at that confidence level. It doesn't prove r = 0 exactly, only that the evidence for a nonzero slope is weak.
